title: Stop Guessing. Here’s How to Build What People Will Actually Pay For
channel: Chris Koerner on The Koerner Office Podcast
promo_conflict: No sponsorship is disclosed. PickFu is explicitly described as not sponsoring the video; Mocha is demonstrated on a paid plan, with no relationship stated.

stated_problem.quote: I need clients to see my calendar.

idea.name: BookFlow dog-groomer booking widget
idea.one_liner: An embeddable appointment booking widget for dog groomers, sold to small businesses; the payment model is not stated.
idea.customer: Dog groomers and, in the broader concept, other small businesses.
idea.offer: A branded website widget for selecting a grooming service, date and time, then submitting customer and pet details.
idea.revenue_model: Direct sale to businesses; price and payment cadence not stated.

key_quotes.quote: We're going to start building an appointment booking widget for websites that we can sell to businesses.
I want to build a widget that small businesses can easily add to their websites that will enable potential customers to book an appointment with them.
Just make one really good appointment booking widget for dog groomers and nothing else.
This is something that real business owners just told me that they want and that they would pay for.

claims.claim: The interim poll had 27 responses.
claims.quote: I've had 27 people respond to my PickFu survey so far.

claims.claim: In the interim tally, appointment booking received 11 votes.
claims.quote: 11 votes for appointment booking, two for contact forms, six for testimonials, six for chatbot, two for pricing calculator.

claims.claim: The completed poll received 100 responses.
claims.quote: I have received all 100 responses to my poll

claims.claim: The Mocha plan used to build the prototype cost $20 per month.
claims.quote: I'm paying for the $20 a month account

claims.claim: The initial build took 4 minutes and 47 seconds and produced 12 changes and 10 files.
claims.quote: it took 4 minutes and 47 seconds to make 12 changes and deliver 10 files.

claims.claim: The prototype demo listed a basic bath and brush at $45 for 60 minutes; this is demo data, not a reported market rate.
claims.quote: It shows basic bath and brush, 60 minutes, 45 bucks.

claims.claim: The prototype demo listed a full groom package at $75 for 90 minutes; this is demo data, not a reported market rate.
claims.quote: Full groom package, 75 bucks, 90 minutes.

claims.claim: The prototype demo listed a nail trim at $15 for 15 minutes; this is demo data, not a reported market rate.
claims.quote: Or nail trim only, 15 bucks and 15 minutes.

claims.claim: The multi-prompt website build took about 18 minutes.
claims.quote: It took about 18 minutes flat.

claims.claim: The working appointment app took about 20 minutes or less to produce.
claims.quote: especially since it took about 20 minutes if not less.

claims.claim: The speaker estimates US development teams would charge at least $10,000 for comparable work.
claims.quote: If you hire them here in the States, it's going to cost you at least $10,000.

claims.claim: The speaker estimates overseas development teams would charge at least $5,000 for comparable work.
claims.quote: Overseas, like the Philippines or Ukraine, at least $5,000.

claims.claim: The speaker says an idea could become a working product ready to sell by noon, starting at 9 a.m.
claims.quote: You can have an idea at 9:00 a.m. and have a working product ready to sell by noon, by lunch.

claims.claim: The speaker describes the poll-to-prototype process as taking 16 minutes.
claims.quote: From poll to prototype in 16 minutes.

claims.claim: The speaker says a poll could cost hundreds of dollars on PickFu, though he does not give an exact price.
claims.quote: you don't have to pay PickFu hundreds of dollars to run a poll.

claims.claim: The speaker says adapting the app to tree-trimming companies would take one prompt; this is an unverified estimate.
claims.quote: if I wanted to make this an appointment setting app for tree trimming companies, one prompt and I'm done.

acquisition_channels.details: Proposed using ads to sell widgets to a specific industry; no campaign or sales results are reported.

ideas.delivery: A business embeds and configures the booking widget on its website. Customers select a service, date and time, then submit contact and pet details.

prices: Prototype demo: $45 basic bath and brush, $75 full groom, $15 nail trim
At least $10,000 US development cost estimate; at least $5,000 overseas estimate

ideas.other_uk_rules: UK GDPR applies to personal data collected in bookings, such as names, email addresses, phone numbers and notes. If sold as a recurring subscription, check DMCC Act subscription-contract requirements.

stated_problem.quote: Because of that, they believe it must be expensive.
stated_problem.speaker: Chris Koerner

idea.name: Industry-specific website chatbot
idea.one_liner: A chatbot for a specific industry that answers website visitors' questions from the site's pages and is sold to businesses; price and payment model are unstated.
idea.customer: Businesses in a specific, unnamed industry.
idea.offer: A website chatbot layer that answers questions using the business's pages.
idea.revenue_model: Sell to businesses; price and payment cadence not stated.

key_quotes.quote: building an appointment booking widget and a chatbot, and then using ads to try to sell these to a specific industry.
Half of people think chatbots are annoying. The other half think that they're magic.
people think chatbots are the hardest thing to build.
there's a signal that the people that ranked it first are the most willing not just to pay, but to pay a lot for it
you add a simple chatbot layer that answers questions using the website's pages.

claims.claim: The interim poll tally showed six votes for chatbots.
claims.quote: 11 votes for appointment booking, two for contact forms, six for testimonials, six for chatbot, two for pricing calculator.

claims.claim: In the completed poll, chatbot and appointment booking tied for first.
claims.quote: appointment booking was clearly number one, but it ended as tied for first with a chatbot.

claims.claim: The speaker says half of respondents found chatbots annoying and half thought they were good.
claims.quote: Half of people think chatbots are annoying. The other half think that they're magic.

claims.claim: The speaker says respondents believed chatbots must be expensive because they seemed difficult to build.
claims.quote: Because of that, they believe it must be expensive.

claims.claim: The speaker infers that respondents ranking chatbots first would be willing to pay a lot.
claims.quote: there's a signal that the people that ranked it first are the most willing not just to pay, but to pay a lot for it

acquisition_channels.details: Proposed using ads to sell the chatbot to a specific industry; no campaign or sales results are reported.

ideas.delivery: A website chatbot layer answers questions using the business's website pages. The transcript does not describe a completed chatbot or its operating workflow.
ideas.other_uk_rules: UK GDPR may apply if chatbot conversations collect or process personal data. If sold as a recurring subscription, check DMCC Act subscription-contract requirements.
